g9-history-uh7-t1.overview: In 1270 Yekuno-Amlak restored a dynasty that claimed descent from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba and ruled the Christian highland kingdom for centuries. This lesson examines its legendary legitimacy, its expansion, its royal prison and its gult land system.
objectives: Explain how Yekuno-Amlak founded the 'Solomonic' dynasty in 1270 and why the name is placed in quotation marks
Describe the territorial expansion of the Christian kingdom under Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-1344)
Analyse the political role of the royal prison at Amba-Gishen after 1300
Explain why the medieval kings ruled through mobile capitals instead of a permanent capital
Describe the gult and rist land system and the Church-state relationship of the period
g9-history-uh7-t1.simple: Yekuno-Amlak, a local ruler of Amhara, came to power in 1270 and claimed descent from the Aksumite kings. He called his dynasty 'Solomonic' and used the legend of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon to argue that the Zagwe rulers had been illegitimate. The claim was written down in the Kibre Negest in the 14th century. In 1270 the kingdom covered only southern Eritrea, Tigray, Lasta and northern Shewa, but Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-1344) expanded it in every direction. Because the court needed daily food and firewood, the kings ruled from mobile camps rather than one capital. Officials were paid with gult rights to collect tribute, while peasants held rist land. Church and state grew closely tied.
g9-history-uh7-t1.detailed:
Founding and legitimacy. Yekuno-Amlak, a local ruler in Amhara, restored the dynasty in 1270. He claimed to be a descendant of the Aksumite kings, and he and his followers took the name 'Solomonic' to justify their legitimacy by arguing that the Zagwe rulers were illegitimate. The name is placed in quotation marks because the claim of descent from King Solomon of Israel is legendary and cannot be historically proven. It was elaborated in the Kibre Negest ('Glory of Kings') in the 14th century, which claimed that the Ethiopian ruling class descended from Menilek I, son of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon. Monarchs from Yekuno-Amlak to Emperor Haile Silassie I claimed descent from Menilek I.

Territorial expansion. In 1270 the Christian kingdom was confined to southern Eritrea, Tigray, Lasta and northern Shewa. Yekuno-Amlak and his successors, especially Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-1344), expanded from this base. Amde-Tsion was the first 'Solomonic' king to follow a wider and rapid territorial expansion policy. The kingdom's limits came to cover the highland provinces of Aksum and Zagwe in the north, Gondar and eastern Gojjam in the north-west, Bizamo and Damot in the south-west, the Gurage lands and the Omotic populations of Wolaita and Gamo in the south, and Ifat, Fatagar, Dawaro, Hadiya and Bali in the east and south-east.

Motive and the Zeila trade. Expansion was driven by economic and political motives, above all to control trade routes and seize territory. Control over the Zeila trade route helped Yekuno-Amlak strengthen his economic power; that wealth in turn allowed him to organize and sustain a strong army. The flow of commodities to the coast grew, and this economic and military strength helped Amde-Tsion defeat his opponents and enlarge his kingdom.

The royal prison and succession. After Yekuno-Amlak's reign ended in 1285, political instability caused constant power struggles among his sons and grandsons. The problem was partly resolved in 1300, during the reign of Widim-Ra'ad (r. 1299-1314), by the establishment of a royal prison at Amba-Gishen in present-day southern Wollo. The royal family's male members were kept there under soldiers loyal to the reigning monarch. When a monarch died, court dignitaries sent an army to the prison to escort the designated heir to the throne. This practice lasted until Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi's force destroyed Amba-Gishen in 1540.

Mobile capitals. From 1270 until Gondar was established in 1636, the medieval monarchs had no permanent capital such as Aksum or Lalibela. They ruled a vast territory through mobile courts, at first centred around Lake Haiq in today's South Wollo. The court then shifted southward to Menz, Tegulet and Bulga in northern Shewa, and finally to eastern Shewa around the heights of Yerer and Zequalla. Mobile camps were needed to obtain daily food and firewood for the large number of officials, soldiers and servants. The camps impoverished their own surroundings, caused deforestation and water and air pollution, and were then abandoned; this made stable capitals difficult and kept the court moving.

The gult and rist system. To administer this vast territory the kingdom consolidated a feudal system of administration known as the gult system. State officials received the gult right, the right to share the produce of the peasantry, and its holder was called a bale-gult or gult owner. The bale-gult collected tribute in kind, used peasant labour, and could recruit and command a local army; in return he maintained law and order in his area. Rist right, by contrast, was a claim to the hereditary ownership of land, a communal birthright. The state provided security, while the peasants were obliged to pay tribute, or gibber, to the state. Gult right was a medieval substitute for salary: it lasted only as long as the official remained loyal and was not hereditary.

Church and state. Like the Zagwe rulers, the 'Solomonic' kings maintained the political and cultural traditions of Aksum and continued to expand Christianity. The rulers exercised political and religious power at the same time, and the Church-state relationship became very strong, almost reaching its peak. The kings continued the Zagwe tradition of foreign relations with Egypt and the Middle East and extended them to Europe, establishing closer ties with Portugal and Spain.

workedExamples.problem: Was the 'Solomonic' dynasty really descended from King Solomon, as its supporters claimed?
workedExamples.given: The dynasty came to power in 1270, claimed descent from Menilek I, son of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon, and recorded the claim in the Kibre Negest in the 14th century.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: distinguish a legendary claim that gives legitimacy from evidence that can be historically proven.
workedExamples.substitution: The Kibre Negest is a later text that repeats the claim, and no contemporary source proves a descent from Solomon.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the only support for the claim is legend and a much later book, historians treat it as an unproven claim of legitimacy.
workedExamples.answer: The descent was a legend used to legitimize rule, not a historically proven fact; that is why the name 'Solomonic' is written in quotation marks.

workedExamples.problem: Why did the Christian kings rule from mobile courts between 1270 and 1636?
workedExamples.given: No permanent capital existed from 1270 until Gondar was established in 1636; the court moved for food, firewood and military reasons.
workedExamples.formula: Historical reasoning: identify the causes of a practice and then trace its consequences.
workedExamples.substitution: Large numbers of officials, soldiers and servants needed daily supplies, and one place could not provide them for long.
workedExamples.calculation: Moving to food supply areas impoverished the surroundings, which forced the camp to move again, so the practice repeated itself.
workedExamples.answer: The kings moved because a large court could not be supplied from one place, and the damage the camp did to its surroundings kept it moving.

workedExamples.problem: How did the gult system help the king govern a vast territory?
workedExamples.given: The bale-gult collected tribute, used peasant labour and could raise a local army, but had to maintain law and order in his area.
workedExamples.formula: Concept: indirect rule through local officials divides a large state into smaller units.
workedExamples.substitution: Officials were paid with the right to collect tribute instead of a salary, so they governed on the state's behalf.
workedExamples.calculation: Because each official governed his own area in return for service, the empire was administered without a large central bureaucracy.
workedExamples.answer: The gult system turned officials into paid local governors and gave the kingdom a large territorial army at low central cost.

g9-history-uh7-t1.summary: Yekuno-Amlak restored the dynasty in 1270 and justified it with the legendary descent from King Solomon, written down in the Kibre Negest. Under Amde-Tsion (r. 1314-1344) the Christian kingdom expanded in all directions, driven by the desire to control the Zeila trade. Succession was managed through the royal prison at Amba-Gishen after 1300, and the vast realm was governed by mobile courts and the gult and rist land system, with a very close Church-state relationship.

g9-history-uh7-t2.overview: After Islam reached the Horn, a chain of Muslim sultanates grew along the long-distance trade routes, above all the Zeila route. This lesson locates the main sultanates, explains the rise of Ifat under the Walasma dynasty and follows the birth of Adal around Harar.
objectives: Identify the Muslim sultanates that emerged along the long-distance trade routes
Explain how the Zeila trade route linked the states and peoples of Ethiopia and the Horn
Describe the rise of Ifat under the Walasma dynasty and its defeat in 1332
Locate smaller sultanates such as Fatagar, Dawaro, Bali and Hadiya
Explain the founding and later shift of the Sultanate of Adal
g9-history-uh7-t2.simple: The spread of Islam into Ethiopia and the Horn was followed by the rise of many Muslim sultanates along the long-distance trade routes. Along the Zeila route, the most important gateway of Islam to the interior, states such as Ifat, Fatigar, Dawaro, Dara, Bali, Hadya, Arbabini, Sharka and Adal were formed. Ifat emerged south of Shewa towards the middle of the 13th century under Umar Walasma, founder of the Walasma dynasty. In 1285 it destroyed the older Makhzumite dynasty and controlled most of the profitable Zeila trade, becoming the strongest rival of the Christian highland state. After Ifat was defeated in 1332, a branch of the Walasma family founded the Sultanate of Adal around Harar in 1367.
g9-history-uh7-t2.detailed:
Islam and the trade routes. The establishment of several Muslim sultanates along the long-distance trade routes followed the introduction of Islam to Ethiopia and the Horn. The Zeila trade route served as the most important gateway of Islam to the interior of Ethiopia, and a series of Muslim states formed along it. Some of these sultanates were Ifat, Fatigar, Dawaro, Dara, Bali, Hadya, Arbabini, Sharka and Adal.

The rise of Ifat. Towards the middle of the 13th century a Muslim sultanate, Ifat, emerged to the south of Shewa. Its founder was Umar Walasma, and so its ruling house is called the Walasma dynasty. In 1285 AD Ifat destroyed the older Makhzumite dynasty and became the strongest Muslim sultanate in the region. It controlled a vast territory through which the long-distance trade routes of Zeila passed, so most of the profitable Zeila trade came under its control. Eventually Ifat became the strongest rival of the Christian highland state.

Competition and the defeat of Ifat. Since 1270 the Christian highland state also developed a great interest in the Zeila trade and its routes. Control of the Zeila trade therefore became the primary source of conflict between the two states. Frequent skirmishes finally resulted in the defeat of Ifat by the Christian forces of Amde Seyon in 1332 AD.

The smaller sultanates. Several other small Muslim sultanates lay to the south, east and north of Ifat. Fatagar emerged around the middle of the 13th century and was situated south of the present-day Bulga around Shenkora. Dawaro was located between the middle Awash River and the upper Wabe-Shebele. Bali lay in the rich area south of the Wabe-Shebele, though we do not know when it emerged as a state. Dara probably existed between Dawaro and Bali. Arbabini lay between Dawaro and Hadiya, about which very little is known. Hadiya was located to the west of Dawaro and Bali and was first mentioned during the reign of Amde Seyon. Sharka was located in the present territory of Arsi; from the 14th century onwards it existed as a tributary to the Christian kingdom until the first quarter of the 16th century.

Trade as a cause and a source of conflict. Trade was one of the most significant factors in the rise and development of these states. It served as a significant source of livelihood and acted as a major agent in the formation of Muslim sultanates. At the same time it remained a major source of conflict between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim sultanates. After its establishment, Ifat conducted a series of campaigns against its neighbouring sultanates, extending its hegemony over these areas, and it also resisted the expansion of the Christian kingdom.

The founding of Adal. One branch of the Walasma family realized that Ifat was becoming an easy target for the Christian kingdom because of its location. It therefore moved further to the south-eastern lowlands and established a new and vigorous Muslim sultanate, Adal, in the highland districts around Harar in 1367. The first centre of this extended Walasma dynasty was at a place called Dakar, located south-east of Harar. The family consolidated its power there and began another phase of military campaigns against the frontiers of the Christian kingdom.

Later movement of the Adal centre. In 1520 the centre of Adal was changed to the city of Harar. After the defeat of Imam Ahmed in 1543 and under pressure from the Oromo population movement, the sultanate was forced to change its capital to Awsa in 1576/7, in the present Afar region. Adal became a centre of resistance against the Christian kingdom until the second half of the sixteenth century.

g9-history-uh7-t3.overview: The rivalry over long-distance trade reached its height between 1529 and 1543 in the wars of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi against the Christian kingdom. This lesson explains the causes, the main battles, the foreign intervention of Ottoman Turkey and Portugal, and the lasting effects of the conflict.
objectives: Explain the economic and political causes of conflict between the Christian kingdom and Adal
Trace the campaigns of Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi from 1527 to 1543
Describe the intervention of Ottoman Turkey and Portugal and its consequences
Assess the role of women such as Bati Del Wanbara and Queen mother Seble-Wongel
Evaluate the political, economic and social impacts of the wars on both states
g9-history-uh7-t3.simple: The main cause of conflict in Ethiopia and the Horn was the desire to control long-distance trade, especially the profitable Zeila route, together with territorial expansion. The height of the war came between 1529 and 1543. After Ifat was defeated in 1332, resistance was rebuilt, and leadership later came from Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, born at Hubet between Dire Dawa and Jigjiga. His expeditions against Lebne Dengel began in 1527, and in March 1529 he won at Shimbra Kure near Mojjo. By 1535 his empire stretched from Zeila to Massawa. Ottoman Turkey supported the Imam, while Portugal helped the Christian side. On 25 February 1543 the Imam was killed at the battle of Woyna-Dega, and Emperor Gelawdewos regained the plateau, though he himself was killed by Emir Nur in 1559.
g9-history-uh7-t3.detailed:
The causes of the conflict. The primary source of conflict among peoples and states in Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa was the desire to monopolize long-distance trade, which was a source of great wealth and a link among the peoples of the region. The desire for territorial expansion was a second source of rivalry. The revival of long-distance trade caused competition between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim principalities, and the height of the war came between 1529 and 1543. In the beginning the Zeila route was under the control of the Muslim states, mainly Ifat, but in 1332 Ifat was defeated and lost its independence, so the monopoly passed to Amde Seyon.

Rebuilding resistance. To regain their independence and control over the Zeila trade route, Haqadin II and Sa'adadin retreated to the Harar plateau and set up a new Muslim resistance base in the late fourteenth century. Later, internal strife, corruption and anarchy intensified among the Muslim sultanates and new leadership was urgently called for. Such leadership came from Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, also named 'the left-handed'. His origin is obscure: he was born at Hubet between Dire Dawa and Jigjiga and was raised by his devout Muslim kin in one of the oases on the route to Zeila.

Mobilisation and early victories. After Imam Ahmad came to power, battles were fought for control of the long-distance trade routes through Zeila. One of his notable achievements was that he mobilized the pastoral communities of Afar, Argoba, Somali, Harari and others for a common cause, persuading them to cooperate instead of fighting among themselves, and consolidated his army to fight the Christian kingdom. His military expeditions against the forces of Lebne Dengel started in 1527. Recognizing the danger, Lebne Dengel gathered a massive force in 1528, but a logistical problem prevented the Christian army from defeating Adal. In March 1529 the Muslim force of Imam Ahmad won victory over the Christian army at the battle of Shimbra Kure, near the present town of Mojjo.

The empire at its height. The Imam's forces went on to win further victories and controlled territories including Bali, Dawaro, Fatagar, Sidama, Hadiya and Kambata, so that the Christian kingdom was at risk. By 1535 Imam Ahmad's empire stretched from Zeila to Massawa on the coast, including the Ethiopian interior. As he penetrated deep into the Christian kingdom, the Imam established a civil and administrative bureaucracy made up of his own men and new recruits from the Christian territories. One of the most helpful figures during the war was the wife of the Imam, Bati Del Wanbara, daughter of the Muslim military commander of Adal known as Mahfuz; she accompanied her husband throughout his expeditions.

Foreign intervention. The conflict took on an international dimension when Portugal and Ottoman Turkey intervened for their own advantage. Since the twelfth century Europeans had found the long-distance route from Europe to the Far East blocked by the Ottoman Turks, and Ottoman Turkey was an established power in the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean; the Portuguese wanted new bases on those coasts. Having noticed the diplomatic missions between the Christian kingdom and Portugal, the Turks gave moral and military support to Imam Ahmad, who received Turkish musketeers in 1540. Meanwhile, following Lebne Dengel's earlier request of 1535, Portuguese soldiers arrived at the Christian court in 1541. However, in August 1542 the Christian army was defeated at Ofla in today's southern Tigray, where about two hundred Portuguese and their leader Christopher da Gama were killed.

The battle of Woyna-Dega and after. Under Emperor Gelawdewos, preparations for the decisive clash were made, and the Queen mother, Seble-Wongel, advised the reigning emperor how to prepare. Imam Ahmad's army could no longer use its previous quality. On 25 February 1543, while the Imam was encamped near Lake Tana, he was attacked and killed after fierce fighting at the battle of Woyna-Dega, where Adal's forces were defeated by the combined troops of Gelawdewos and the Portuguese. The defeated troops of Adal, including the Imam's wife Bati Del Wanbara, retreated to Adal. Gelawdewos regained control of practically the whole northern and central plateau, and to encourage national reconciliation he was tolerant toward the highland Muslim populations that submitted to him.

Revenge, effects and interaction. Controlling the Muslim-dominated areas was not easy. Under the leadership of Nur Ibn al-Waazir Mujahid, Adal prepared to wage war for revenge, and in 1559 Emir Nur's army clashed with Gelawdewos and killed the king himself. The wars had many impacts: both states were exhausted and weakened by the loss of enormous human and material wealth, which paved the way for the easy success of the Oromo population movement. At the same time, people from different cultural groups intermarried and engaged in linguistic and religious interactions. Between 1529 and 1543 the sultanate dominated not only the Christian kingdom but parts of the Horn; nevertheless in 1543 the Christian kingdom regained its freedom, and Islam gained new converts in parts of the heartland. Trade continued to be the major channel of social integration, as merchants moved between the highlands and the coast, and this interdependence in economic, social, cultural and political spheres laid the foundation for modern Ethiopia.

g9-history-uh7-t4.overview: Central and southern Ethiopia held many states and peoples with indigenous religions, including Damot, Kafa, Ennarya, Bizamo, Wolaita, Kambata, the Gurage chiefdoms and the Agaw kingdom of Gojjam. This lesson describes their politics, economy and gradual incorporation into or independence from the Christian highland kingdom.
objectives: Identify the states and peoples of central and southern Ethiopia in the period
Explain the early importance of Damot and its annexation in 1316
Describe the Agaw kingdom of Gojjam and its incorporation by Amde Tsiyon
Analyse the trade and agriculture on which the southern and central economies rested
Describe the less centralized societies of the frontier lowlands
g9-history-uh7-t4.simple: In the central and southern parts of the region there were states and peoples with indigenous religions: Damot, Kafa, Ennarya, Bizamo, Walaita, Yem, Kambata, the Gurage chiefdoms and the Agaw kingdom of Gojjam. Damot was probably the earliest and may have existed since Aksumite times. Its best-known ruler, Motalami, was converted to Christianity by Abune Tekle Haymanot in the late thirteenth century, and King Amde Seyon annexed Damot in 1316. Kafa was an independent kingdom known since the end of the fourteenth century, while Wolaita paid tribute to King Yeshaq (r. 1413-1430) and its dynasty was called Wolaita-Malla. The Agaw kingdom of Gojjam, south of Lake Tana, was incorporated by Amde Tsiyon in the early fourteenth century. These economies rested on trade and agriculture, trading enslaved people, civets and ivory.
g9-history-uh7-t4.detailed:
States with indigenous religions. In the central and southern parts of the region there were states and peoples with indigenous religions. Those were Damot, Kafa, Ennarya, Bizamo, Walaita, Yem, Kambata, the Gurage chiefdoms and the Agaw kingdom of Gojjam.

Damot. Damot was probably the earliest of these states and seems to have existed as early as the Aksumite period over an extensive territory that included the areas south of the Blue Nile River. It may possibly have extended to include the areas of Enareya, Bizamo and Walaita. Among its rulers the well-known one was called Motalami, who was converted to Christianity by Abune Tekle Haymanot in the late thirteenth century AD. The rulers of the 'Solomonic' dynasty began attempts to bring Damot under their control in the last quarter of the thirteenth century, and finally King Amde Seyon annexed it into the Christian state in 1316.

Bizamo, Enareya and Kafa. Information on the history of Bizamo is scanty, but there is evidence that it had early connections with Damot. The kingdom of Enareya probably existed in the area north of the Gojeb River, and the influence of the highland Christian state seems to have extended into the area through Damot. Enareya became part of the Christian highland kingdom, and its rulers built several churches. South of Enareya was the kingdom of Kafa, known at least since the end of the fourteenth century. Kafa was not mentioned in any of the Christian documents and remained an independent kingdom from the Christian highland state.

Wolaita and the Gurage chiefdoms. The state of Wolaita may also have been part of the kingdom of Damot, since its connection with Damot was strong. The ruling dynasty of Wolaita was known as Wolaita-Malla. Wolaita was mentioned as one of the areas paying tribute to the Christian king Yeshaq (r. 1413-1430), and it may have continued as part of the Christian empire up to the wars of Ahmad ibn Ibrahim. The Gurage chiefdoms were concentrated in the area west of Lake Zeway and the highlands of Dawaro, and their local chiefs used the titles of Azmach, Abegaz and Nigus.

The Agaw kingdom of Gojjam. The Agaw kingdom of Gojjam was mentioned in the Christian historical documents. It was located to the south of Lake Tana and exercised strong control over the Lake and its islands. Many Christian kings made successive attempts to bring it under their control, advancing to the hinterlands using the Lake Tana region as a steppingstone. Finally Amde Tsiyon (r. 1314-1344) incorporated Gojjam into the Christian state in the early fourteenth century. In his reign a Christian preacher at one of the island monasteries of Lake Tana, named Abba Za Yohannes, marched southwards to the Agaw villages and tried to evangelize the people. The Agaw community of the island and the surrounding area had already been converted during the Zagwe period, but the people south of the Lake were predominantly followers of the indigenous religion, and the preaching immediately led to open conflict with Zhan Chuhay, the ruler of the Agaw kingdom that extended south-east as far as Amadamit Mountain in what is today Quarit. Zhan Chuhay ordered his army to arrest Abba ZeYohannes, and the monk was detained at Amadamit Mountain. Amde Tsiyon then dispatched his forces; Zhan Chuhay was killed in the campaign and Abba ZeYohannes was freed. This marked the incorporation of the Gojjam Agaw kingdom into the Christian highland kingdom. After the conquest the title of 'King of Gojjam' was maintained by local rulers under the Christian state, Christianity was introduced to Gojjam, its people were Christianized, and churches and monasteries were built in the kingdom.

Economy. The economy of the peoples and states of southern and central Ethiopia was based on profits from trade and agriculture. The main trade items were enslaved people, civets, ivory and other natural products. There was high demand for enslaved people from this region in Arabia, Persia and India, and slaves as captives of war were obtained from the south and central regions and from the highland Christian territories.

Less centralized societies. Besides these peoples with a state tradition, other societies lived in the same area without highly organized states. Most of them inhabited the frontier areas of present-day Ethiopia and its neighbours, and less centralized communities lived in the narrow lowland strip in the west along the Ethio-Sudanese border. These peoples were mainly speakers of the Nilo-Saharan language family. They possessed their own local administrative system, were led by their chiefs and local elderly councils based on their villages and clan territories, and were the primary agents of frontier trade and cultural relations between the Ethiopian interior and its neighbours.

g9-history-uh7-t5.overview: Wars and population movements dominated the Horn in the sixteenth century. This lesson explains the movements of the Argoba, Afar and Somali, the great Oromo expansion of 1522-1618, and the adoption systems by which newcomers and local peoples were integrated.
objectives: Explain the causes and consequences of population movement in Ethiopia and the Horn
Describe the movements of the Argoba, Afar and Somali peoples
Trace the directions and two phases of the Oromo population movement
Identify the twelve Butta wars and the Gadaa centres established during the expansion
Assess the reasons for the success of the Oromo movement and its integration of peoples
g9-history-uh7-t5.simple: In the sixteenth century the Horn was dominated by wars and population movements. The Argoba, Afar and Somali moved because of the conflict between the Christian kingdom and Adal in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, but the largest movement was that of the Oromo. The Oromo are an indigenous Cushitic people whose original homeland, according to oral tradition, lay in the south-eastern highlands, with Madda Walabu as their political and religious centre. Demographic pressure and the wars pushed them out between 1522 and 1618. The Barentu moved north-east and the Borana north-west in two phases, through twelve Butta wars. The Gadaa system, mass participation, the horse and the exhaustion of the two warring states explain their success, and through Moggasa and Guddifacha they adopted other peoples, producing lasting ethnic and cultural mixing.
g9-history-uh7-t5.detailed:
An age of movement. In the sixteenth century the history of the Horn of Africa was dominated by wars and population movements, which played important roles in shaping the history of Ethiopia and the Horn. The Argoba, Afar and Somali movements occurred as a result of the conflicts between the Christian kingdom and the Sultanate of Adal in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. However, the largest population movement and expansion of the period was that of the Oromo.

The Argoba. The territory of the Argoba lay in the region where the major caravan trade routes pass to Zeila, so the Argoba were major agents of trade and of Muslim sultanate formation in the Horn, such as Shewa and Ifat. Their homeland was also a target of the Christian kingdom's expansion, and the Sultanate of Ifat, in which the Argoba were dominant, became a centre of resistance against the Christian kingdom. The Argoba joined the Afar and the Somali against the Christian kingdom and were therefore affected by the consequences of wars since the thirteenth century. The lasting effect of the wars can be seen in the dispersed settlement of the Argoba people. The Afar and the Somali. Due to drought, the Afar moved towards the east until they reached the middle Awash. Trade routes linking the ports of the Horn passed through Afar territory, so the region became a centre of competition between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim sultanates. Besides being actors in the conflict, the Afar were pressured by it to move in different directions to avoid the risk of disputes, and in the sixteenth century their pastoral economy helped them survive the destructive effects of the wars. The Somali lived in an area crossed by important trade routes, and before the wars of Imam Ahmad there was strong demographic pressure from the Somali. Their population movement was a strong force behind the military strength of the Imam, but it did not last long, as they returned to their home base after his defeat in 1543.

The Oromo homeland and causes. The Oromo are an indigenous Cushitic people of Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa. When Aksum came into history it was clear that the Oromo also occupied a considerable part of the land. According to Oromo oral traditions, the original homeland of the Oromo before the sixteenth century was the south-eastern part of Ethiopia's highlands, and the political and religious centre of the Oromo settlement area was Madda Walabu, located on the Bale-Sidama borderlands. A combination of natural and manmade factors caused the movement in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: demographic pressure and the consequent need for land for a growing human and livestock population, and the conflict between the Christian kingdom and the Muslim sultanates, which forced the Oromo to leave the lands they inhabited.

Confederacies, directions and phases. The Barentu and the Borana were the two main confederacies that made up the Oromo people before they began to move. The Mecha, Tulama, southern Borana and Guji clans made up the Borana confederacy, while the Karayu, Marawa, Ittu, Humbana, Akachu, Wollo and Arsi clans made up the Barentu. The years 1522 to 1618 saw the time of movement and expansion. Inside the Ethiopian region the movement was mostly set in two directions: the Barentu headed north-east, while the Borana took a north-westerly direction; outside the region they also moved towards Kenya and Somalia. There were two phases: a first, early sixteenth-century phase of modest and gradual movement, and a second phase lasting from the middle of the sixteenth century to 1618. Force was used to carry out this massive movement. The Oromo headed north, passed through a corridor between Mount Walabu and Lake Abaya, turned westward halfway between Lakes Abaya and Hawassa, crossed the Bilatte River, and then travelled northward towards the lakes of the Rift Valley.

The twelve Butta wars. From 1522 to 1618 the Oromo fought twelve Butta wars. The first Gadaa, Melba (1522-1530), defeated the Christian regiment Batra Amora led by Fasil and occupied Bali. Mudena (1530-8) reached the edge of the Awash River. Kilole (1538-46) controlled Dawaro after defeating the Christian regiment Adal Mabraq. Bifole (1546-54) advanced to Waj and Erer. Michille (1554-62) won victories over Hamalmal's force at Dago, the Jan Amora forces, and Adal led by Emir Nur Mujahiddin at Mount Hazalo. Harmufa (1562-70) fought Minas (r. 1559-63) at Qacina and Wayyata and occupied Angot, Ganzyi and Sayint. In 1574 Sartsa Dingil's (r. 1563-97) cavalry, led by Azzaj Halibo, defeated Robale Gadaa (1570-78) at Woyna Daga, though Robale recovered by defeating Zara'a Yohannis' force. Birmaji (1578-86) controlled Ar'ine in Waj, crossed Jama to Wolaqa and overwhelmed the Daragoti regiment. Mul'ata (1586-94) seized Damot, Bizamo, Gafat, Dambiya and Tigray. In the early seventeenth century Dulo (1594-1602), Melba (1603-10) and Mudena (1610-18) expanded to the western and northern parts of the Horn, while others such as the Warday moved to Kenya and to Bur Haqaba and Majertin in Somalia.

Gadaa centres and the reasons for success. In their movement into various regions, different Oromo branches established Gadaa centres, among them Oda Nabee of Tulama in East Shewa, Oda Roba of Sikko-Mando in Arsi, Oda Bultum of Itu-Humbenna in Hararge, Oda Bisil of Mecha in West Shewa and Oda Bulluq of Jawwi Mecha in Horro-Guduru, as well as Gayo of Sabbo-Gona, Me'e Bokko of Guji, Oda Dogi of Ilu, Oda Hulle of Jimma and Oda Garad of Wallo. Gadaa leaders such as Dawe Gobbo of Borana, Anna Sorra of Guji, Makko-Bili of Mecha and Babbo Koyye of Jimma established Gadaa centres and laid down cardinal laws in their areas. The various Oromo groups kept their relations through the office of Abba Muda (the father of anointment) seated at Madda Walabu, and sent delegates to the central chaffe there until the pan-Oromo assembly was forbidden in 1900. The movement succeeded for several reasons: the Gadaa system provided training and military organisation; almost all members of society participated in the wars; it was a large-scale expansion difficult to stop; the Oromo made wide and good use of the horse; the institution of adaptation helped; and the movement took place when the Christian kingdom and Adal were exhausted by the wars of the first half of the sixteenth century.

Consequences and integration. The Oromo population movement and expansion brought fundamental changes to the Ethiopian region. Ethnic and cultural intermixing took place between the Oromo and other peoples. The expanding Oromo destroyed the old states of Damot, Bizamo and Ennarya, and the peoples of Damot and Gafat were either assimilated with the Oromo or forced to move from the south to the north and intermingle with the Christian community. The Christian kingdom was greatly disturbed: its territorial and financial strength was weakened, and it was forced to shift its political centre from Shewa in the south to the Lake Tana area and Gondar. The Sultanate of Adal was reduced to the walled town of Harar, where Emir Nur built a wall known as the Jegol Gimb; this ended an age-old conflict between Adal and the Christian kingdom. Following their movement, the Oromo became largely sedentary agriculturists, and in time the great majority adopted Christianity and Islam and later formed kingdoms of their own. Two adoption mechanisms helped in this integration: Guddifacha, a form of adoption in which a parent adopts a child who then enjoys equal rights with a biological child, and Moggasa, the adoption of non-Oromos, commonly known as Oromsu, by incorporating individuals or groups into a clan through an oath of allegiance. The Abba Gadaa undertook Moggasa on behalf of the clan, and the adopted community or individual shared everything equally with the Oromo and gained protection and material benefits. This culture allowed other peoples to mix with the Oromo and live in peace, and the process contributed to social cohesion, national integration and the revival of long-distance trade, while also producing an exchange of socio-cultural values and institutions.

g9-history-uh7-t6.overview: The Gadaa system was the age-grade based, egalitarian political and social organisation of the Oromo, in which an assembly of the ruling class provided leadership and power passed peacefully every eight years. This lesson explains its structure, offices, principles and the place of women.
objectives: Describe the Gadaa system and its age-grade structure
Explain how the Gadaa system organised political, economic, social and religious life
Identify the main offices of the Gadaa government and their duties
Analyse the democratic principles of Gadaa, including check and balance and power-sharing
Explain the role of the Qallu, the Sinqe institution and the place of women in Gadaa
g9-history-uh7-t6.simple: The Gadaa system was based on age grades and was an egalitarian system in which an assembly, or chaffe, of the ruling Gadaa class led the Oromo nation. It regulated political, economic, social and religious life, including conflict resolution (arara), reparation (Guma) and the protection of women's rights. Ten age grades and five classes operated in parallel. Sons joined the first grade forty years after their fathers and moved up every eight years; eight years made one Gadaa period, five periods a generation and nine generations an era. Power passed peacefully every eight years. The Abba Gadaa led the government with officials such as Abba Bokku, Abba-Dula and Abba Sera, but supreme authority rested with the assembly. Women kept their rights through the Sinqe institution.
g9-history-uh7-t6.detailed:
What the Gadaa system was. The Gadaa system was based on age grades. It was an egalitarian system in which an assembly, or chaffe, of the ruling Gadaa class provided leadership for the Oromo nation. It was developed from knowledge gained by community experience over generations. The system regulated the community's political, economic, social and religious activities, dealing with conflict resolution (arara), reparation (Guma) and the protection of women's rights. It served as a mechanism for enforcing moral conduct, building social cohesion and expressing forms of community culture. Moreover, it was an institution through which the Oromo socially organized themselves, administered their affairs, defended their territories, maintained law and order, and managed their economies. The Oromo had practised the Gadaa system long before the sixteenth-century movement.

Democratic elements. The Gadaa system contained elements of democracy such as periodic succession and power-sharing to prevent one-man rule. Other principles included the representation of all lineages, clans and confederacies. The system organized Oromo society into age grades and generation sets that defined members' social, political and economic responsibilities. In the system, ten age grades and five classes operated in parallel, providing a socio-political framework that institutionalised relationships between seniors and juniors and egalitarian relations among grade members, and helping members of an age-set to develop a consistent and stable sense of self and others.

Time and generations. Sons joined the first grade as members of a Gadaa class (generation class or set) forty years after their fathers and were initiated into the next higher grade every eight years. Eight years represented one Gadaa period, five Gadaa periods or forty years represented one generation, and nine generations represented an era. The political philosophy of Gadaa is based on three main values: terms of eight years, balanced opposition between parties, and power-sharing between higher and lower levels. In the Gadaa system, generation, age, sex and class were the guiding criteria in the division of labour and the sharing of responsibilities. Interruption and revival. The Gadaa system was interrupted and revitalised during various eras because of internal and external factors. For instance, the Borana-Barentu Gadaa was instituted after an interruption of nearly two generations, and it was revived in 1450 at Madda Walabu, which became the central chaffe and seat of the senior Qallu until 1900.

The law-making assembly. The Gumi-Gayo was the assembly of the representatives of the entire society and mainly served as the law-making body. In theory any individual had a right to attend and participate in the deliberation and could bring any matter to the attention of the gumi-gayo. Each class sent a delegation of five people to sit in the legislative body called the Caffe, and new laws to be issued and laws to be repealed or amended were introduced to the Caffe by elders for discussion.

Age grades and offices. The common version of the Oromo age grades and the roles associated with them is as follows: Dabale (birth to 8 years) and Game (9 to 16 years) were the grades of socialization; Folle (17 to 24 years) was for military training, agriculture and similar work; Qondala (25 to 32 years) was for military service; Raba-Dori (33 to 40 years) were candidates for political power; Gadaa (41 to 48 years) were the leaders of the Gadaa government; and Yuba (49 to 80 years) were senior advisors, educators and ritual leaders. The Gadaa assumed power for eight years, and there was a peaceful transfer of political power from one Gadaa class to the other every eight years. The head of the government was known as Abba-Gadaa, literally 'father of the period', who was assisted by several elected representatives from among the generation set. These included Abba Bokku (father of scepter), Abba Chaffe (head of the assembly), Abba-Dula (war leader), Abba Sera (father of law), Abba Alanga (judge), Abba Sa'a (father of treasury) and other councillors. The Abba Gadaa or Abba Bokku served as the spokesman of the reigning set, but he did not have absolute power; the supreme authority rested on the assembly (chaffe), which consisted of all members of the ruling Gadaa class, or those in the sixth Gadaa grade (41 to 48 years).

The Qallu and the place of women. In the Gadaa system the senior Qallu (Abba Muda) played indispensable roles in the transfer of power and in legitimizing the ruling Gadaa class. Women maintained their rights through the Sinqe institution, which helped them to form sisterhood and solidarity. Women from childhood to old age, namely guduru (pre-pubescent), qarre (adolescent and ready for marriage), kalale (wives of Luba and Yuba) and cifire (wives of Gadaamojji and above 80 years), were believed to have sacred power, and they were involved in power transfer, conflict resolution, thanksgiving and other ceremonies. The kalale were also privileged to support and advise the ruling class. The Gadaa system functioned by the cyclical transfer of power from one Gadaa class to the next every eight years, and with minor differences in nomenclature in different parts of Oromo territory there were five Gadaa classes, or generation sets. The Gadaa assembly takes place under a sycamore tree (Odaa), symbolically representing its emphasis on dialogue and consensus.

Principles of Gadaa. The Gadaa system has the principles of check and balance through a regular succession every eight years, division of power among executive, legislative and judicial branches, balanced opposition among five parties, and power-sharing among administrative organs. In addition, it embodies the rule of laws that stand above all, the principle of accountability, the role of confession and impeachment (buqqisu), a period of testing, that is, the time gap between elections and investiture, and the principle of check and balance.

g9-history-uh7-t7.overview: Among the Sidama, Gedeo, Konso and Burji, governance rested on councils of elders, elected leaders and generation sets rather than on a single all-powerful monarch. This lesson describes these egalitarian and often decentralized systems of rule.
objectives: Explain what an egalitarian democracy is and where in Ethiopia it was practised
Describe the Sidama system of the Mote, the Songo and the luwa age grades
Explain the ballee system of the Gedeo and the role of the yaa council
Describe the decentralized political structure of the Konso and its councils of elders
Explain the elective basha system of the Burji and the two types of woma
g9-history-uh7-t7.simple: The Sidama, Gedeo, Konso and Burji practised egalitarian and often decentralized systems of governance. The Sidama were led by a Mote (king) who ruled with a council of elders called the Songo and recognised a ritual leader, the Woma. Their age cycle, the luwa, had an eight-year cycle and five named generations, and their moral code was the halale. The Gedeo had the ballee system, in which the yaa general council elected officials such as the Abba Gadaa. The Konso had no central authority over their three regions; each walled village was ruled by a council of elders called hayyota, chosen by the male members and rotating every eighteen years, with the poqalla as priest and peacemaker. The Burji used the elective basha system and had both hereditary and elected woma leaders.
g9-history-uh7-t7.detailed:
Egalitarian governance. Besides the centralized kingdoms, some peoples of Ethiopia and the Horn governed themselves through egalitarian and decentralized systems in which authority was shared among elders, elected officials and generation sets. The clearest examples in this unit are the Sidama, the Gedeo, the Konso and the Burji.

The Sidama: Mote, Songo and Woma. The Sidama had an indigenous system of governance led by the Mote (king). The Mote exercised political and administrative authority in consultation with a council of elders called the Songo. Songo members would raise any agenda for discussion within the council and submit their decisions to the Mote for approval. Although there was no written constitution, the rules were known by heart through generations and practised accordingly. The Woma was the cultural and ritual leader of Sidama society. The criteria for his election were his ability as a peacemaker, bodily perfection, expressive ability, wisdom and caution. The Woma could not participate in war or cattle raiding, as he was considered a man of peace. He handled cultural matters such as offering sacrifices to the spirits and performed rituals such as circumcision and marriage. The Sidama were grouped into two major clans, Bushe and Maldea, which were in turn subdivided into sub-clans. The Sidama people comprised subtribes, gosa, ruled independently by their king, who was in effect a supreme judge, and by the woma. The woma of the different subtribes made up the woma-songo, the assembly of subtribal kings or judges, which was the highest traditional authority.

The Sidama: luwa age grades and halale. Seniority was closely related to the age cycles of the luwa. The luwa structure had many commonalities with the Oromo Gadaa system and played a fundamental role in initiation rites and in maintaining authority roles. Two terms were used to refer to the elderly: gercho, which refers to a person's age, and cimessiccho, which refers to an elder who has undergone the rite of passage into the status of elderhood. The age grade had an eight-year cycle, and each of the five luwa generations had its name: Fulasa, Wawasa, Darara, Hirbora and Mogisa. Each age group selected its Gadaanna, a leader who would represent the generation for eight years. The passage into elderhood, which gives a man the status of cimessima, took place during the rites of the luwa to which he belonged, and a son could not undergo the initiation before his father. According to the halal, an elder was expected to live according to the halale, a moral standard reflecting the truth by avoiding any form of crime, such as stealing, perjury, corruption and injustice, and by adhering to probity, integrity, honesty and truthfulness. The daily lives of the Sidama were organised around the olla, the village, and the mine manni, the family unit, and the murricha, or elder, had a leadership role at village level; in general, gerontocracy dominated the communal network on all levels.

The Sidama: sera and lower assemblies. The sera were defined as the ruling truth, referred to as halale. Halale proclaimed by the elders was hard to challenge and was often the base for forced consensus. Decision making in the assemblies was always with one voice, and consensus was valued over the open confrontation of opposing ideas, though gender and age limited participation, since only elders and only men had a say. The gare-songo was the council of the mote, who were the kings of the gare, the maximal lineage segment. The mote was partly an inherited position, but there might be a choice between the sons of the former mote. The gare-songo dealt with matters closer to daily life, such as making a disobedient son obedient, matters of loans, and it served as a local court that could impose penalties; those who did not pay their penalties could be excommunicated. Within smaller units such as the haracha and the olla there were also songo assemblies headed by the muriccha, chiefly in charge of services related to deaths and funerals. The sera regulated the communal social structure and interaction and can be seen as unwritten law that was at once the morality and the conscience of the individual and the community, providing social security and a procedure of decision making through consensus.

The Sidama case study of Queen Fura. Sidama tradition refers to a legendary Queen, called Motite in the Sidama language, named Fura. During the reign of Fura the status of males was degraded below that of females. She was said to have been cruel, mistrusted men and asked them to carry out difficult or degrading orders. For example, she asked them to bring an animal that had not been mounted by anyone before, and she ordered men to build a house in the air between the earth and the sky. She also ordered the killing of all elderly males.

The Gedeo ballee system. The Gedeo live in the highlands east of Lake Abaya, bordered north by the Sidama and on the remaining sides by the Guji. Tradition indicates that they are descendants of Derasso, and that there was a close relationship between Derasso and the ancestors of neighbouring Oromo groups such as the Guji and Borana, accounting for the similarities in their social organisation. The area around Haro Walabu, a lake near Dilla town, is believed to be the homeland of the Gedeo, and the movement there is believed to have taken place before the sixteenth century. The Gedeo comprised seven clans. Their traditional governance system is known as ballee. It is based on an age system and has similarities with the Gadaa system of the neighbouring Gujji Oromo. The leaders of the ballee were elected by the general council called Yaa from the ruling age group, and the yaa council was the supreme authority among the Gedeo. All ballee officials were elected by the yaa, and the most important of them was the Abba Gadaa, who gave political, social and ritual leadership to the whole Gedeo. Each of the three Gedeo territorial units was administered by a roga, and these were responsible to the Abba Gadaa.

The Konso and the Burji. The Konso live in a primarily hilly area in south-west Ethiopia, east of the Rift Valley, and they speak an East Highland Cushitic language shared with neighbours such as the Burji, Dirashe and Gawada. Their economy depends on mixed agriculture, producing grains, most importantly sorghum and millet, and a tree crop locally called shelgeda whose leaves are eaten like cabbage; they terraced their hillsides with stones, which made their agriculture sustainable. The Konso had a decentralized political structure in which various people and groups shared authority. The poqalla, a priest, was in charge of the clan's welfare and served as a peacemaker during disputes, and the council of elders and members of the generation set known as tella were also involved in government. Until the late nineteenth century the Konso lived in walled villages called paletas, and there was no central authority acting as a sovereign power over the three regions; each village was ruled by a council of elders called hayyota, selected through the direct participation of male members of the village, and membership was not hereditary but rotated every eighteen years. At the core of Konso socio-political organisation were the clan or lineage group and the generation set, the Tselta. The Konso were divided into nine exogamous clans, and the Tselta had a fixed cycle of years starting from birth, though the number varied across villages. The Burji clans belong to one of two moieties named Dashcha and Jiremalecha. Traditional Burji administration had an elective system known as basha (shumet), under which appointments took place in different ceremonies in which official titles were conferred, including officials titled woma in the womis ceremony, kings in royal coronations, dayna officials in daynoma ceremonies and masha in other appointment ceremonies. The Burji possessed two types of woma: one hereditary spiritual woma and one popular elective political elite, or woma, which came to power through a plebiscite based on personal ability and integrity. The hereditary spiritual woma was known as gan, of which there were two types, saganaka gan, which served as a rainmaker, and banbalinka gan, which was believed to possess powers to control and prevent wars, crop pests and disease. The eldest son succeeded his deceased woma father, and the woma was appointed as a king based upon the number of his supporters, his degree of wealth, his oratory and the fulfilment of the social criteria contained in the traditional basha system of appointments.

workedExamples.problem: Why is the Konso system described as decentralized rather than centralized?
workedExamples.given: There was no central authority acting as a sovereign power over the three regions; each walled village was ruled by a council of elders called hayyota, and membership rotated every eighteen years.
workedExamples.formula: Framework: a centralized system has one supreme authority, while a decentralized one shares authority among many bodies.
workedExamples.substitution: Konso authority was spread across village councils, a priest and a generation set rather than one ruler.
workedExamples.calculation: Because no single institution held sovereignty over all regions, the system is decentralized and egalitarian.
workedExamples.answer: It is decentralized because authority was shared among village councils, the poqalla and the tella rather than held by one central ruler.

workedExamples.problem: How did the Sidama limit and balance the authority of the Mote?
workedExamples.given: The Mote ruled in consultation with the Songo; Songo members raised agenda and submitted decisions for approval; the Woma handled ritual matters; the woma-songo was the highest traditional authority.
workedExamples.formula: Historical reasoning: identify which institutions share power with a ruler.
workedExamples.substitution: The council of elders debated and proposed, while the assembly of subtribal kings and judges stood above daily rule.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the Mote needed the approval of the council and was bounded by the highest assembly, his power was not absolute.
workedExamples.answer: The Mote shared authority with the Songo and was bound by the woma-songo and the ritual role of the Woma, so his power was not absolute.

workedExamples.problem: What does the Burji basha system show about leadership in an egalitarian society?
workedExamples.given: The Burji had a hereditary spiritual woma known as gan and a popular elective political woma chosen by plebiscite based on personal ability and integrity.
workedExamples.formula: Historical skill: compare inherited and elected leadership within one system.
workedExamples.substitution: The matter concerns the non-political spiritual office, while ability decides the political office.
workedExamples.calculation: Because the political leader was chosen rather than simply inherited, leadership depended on public support and personal merit.
workedExamples.answer: It shows that leadership was earned through ability and public support, though the sacred office remained hereditary.

commonMistakes: Assuming all Ethiopian societies were centralized kingdoms with a single powerful king.
Confusing the Sidama Mote (king) with the Woma (ritual and cultural leader).
Mixing up the Gedeo ballee and its yaa council with the Konso hayyota council.
Believing Konso political organisation was highly centralized.
Thinking the Burji basha system was hereditary rather than elective.
Forgetting that Sidama deliberation valued consensus and one voice.
Ignoring the limits placed on participation, such as age and gender in Sidama assemblies.

g9-history-uh7-t7.summary: The Sidama, Gedeo, Konso and Burji governed themselves through egalitarian and often decentralized systems. The Sidama were led by the Mote with the Songo council and the ritual leader the Woma, organised by the eight-year luwa age grades and guided by the moral code of halale. The Gedeo had the ballee system with the supreme yaa council electing officials such as the Abba Gadaa, while the Konso shared authority among village councils called hayyota, the poqalla and the tselta generation set. The Burji used the elective basha system with both hereditary and elected woma, showing leadership based on ability and public support.
